content.text: How do I analyze a hearsay problem?

Follow this framework: (1) Is it an out-of-court statement? Any assertion made outside current proceedings. (2) Is it offered for the truth of the matter asserted? If offered for another purpose (effect on listener, verbal act, circumstantial evidence of state of mind), it's not hearsay. (3) If hearsay, check exemptions first (FRE 801(d)) - prior statements by witness or party opponent admissions. (4) Then check exceptions - FRE 803 (availability immaterial): present sense impression, excited utterance, state of mind, business records, etc. FRE 804 (declarant unavailable): former testimony, dying declaration, statement against interest. (5) Don't forget the residual exception (807) and confrontation clause issues in criminal cases.
What privileges apply in estate planning?

Key privileges in estate planning contexts: (1) Attorney-client privilege - protects confidential communications for legal advice; survives death but may be waived in will contests when testator's intent is at issue. (2) Spousal privileges - testimonial privilege (criminal) and marital communications privilege; death terminates testimonial but communications privilege survives. (3) Accountant-client privilege - varies by state; may apply to tax planning discussions. (4) Clergy-penitent privilege - for spiritual advice. In estate litigation, exceptions often apply: fiduciary exception (beneficiaries may access trust communications), crime-fraud exception, and the testator's intent exception for will contests.
